analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, co-ops, and public-private partnerships build their own broadband even when state laws forbid it.
analysis.headline: Six senators backed the bill, but the Senate Commerce Committee never gave it a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states from banning cities, towns, public-private partnerships, and cooperatives from offering broadband internet service. It would also require public providers to treat competing private companies fairly under local rules, and it would not exempt public networks from normal telecommunications law. The goal is to let communities that private providers pass over or overcharge build their own alternative.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses in the roughly twenty states that restrict public broadband would gain a path to a competing, often cheaper internet option. Rural and low-income communities that private providers have declined to serve, or serve at high prices, would be able to back a city-built, co-op, or partnership network. Local governments, public utilities, and cooperatives would gain legal clarity to enter the broadband business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents in states that ban public broadband

how_it_helps.text: Overrides any state statute or regulation that prohibits public providers, public-private partnerships, or cooperatively organized providers from offering advanced telecommunications (broadband) service, so a community cannot be blocked by state law from building its own network.

Includes an antidiscrimination safeguard: a public provider that regulates competing private companies must apply its ordinances and rules without favoring itself, which addresses the standard objection that government-run networks would rig the rules against private competitors.

Keeps normal federal and state telecommunications rules in place through a savings clause, so public networks would compete under the same legal requirements as private ones rather than getting a carve-out.

Where a public, co-op, or partnership network does get built, residents typically gain a second provider in markets that often have only one or two choices, which is the mechanism by which prices tend to fall.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent private cable and telephone companies would face new public-sector competition in markets state laws currently shield, and could lose subscribers and pricing power. Where networks are publicly financed through municipal bonds or other public debt, local taxpayers would bear the risk if the network's revenues fall short. States that enacted restrictions would lose the authority to make that choice for their cities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent broadband providers; local bond taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Public networks are typically financed with taxpayer-backed bonds or other public debt, and if subscriber numbers fall short, local taxpayers, not the incumbent provider, absorb the losses. The bill enables public provision without adding new safeguards for that financial risk beyond ordinary telecom rules.

The bill preempts state law, taking the decision about whether communities may enter the broadband business away from state legislatures and voters who enacted those restrictions, which raises a federalism objection even for people who like the policy.

Nothing in the bill guarantees any network actually gets built; it removes a legal barrier, and communities in sparsely populated areas could still find construction costs too high for a public or co-op network to pencil out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is concrete: in markets with one or two providers, a public or co-op competitor is one of the few forces that reliably lowers prices, and the bill's fairness and savings-clause provisions respond directly to the most common good-faith objections. The downside is real but conditional: taxpayer-financed networks can fail and stick local residents with the debt, and preemption overrides state choices. On balance, the costs are risks that willing communities could weigh for themselves, which is exactly the choice state bans currently take away.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the Community Broadband Act on April 19, 2023, with five original cosponsors: Democrats Blumenthal, Markey, and Wyden, and independents King and Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action of any kind is listed: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone companies are better off, because the state laws that shield them from public and co-op competition remain in force. No consumer in a ban state gained anything from this outcome.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee (Chair Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies
against.what_they_did: Have long backed state laws restricting municipal broadband, the restrictions this bill would void.

sides.party_line_note: All six Senate supporters were Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.note: State-level bans on municipal broadband protect these companies from public, co-op, and partnership competition in their service areas. The bill removes that shield, exposing them to new competitors and downward pressure on prices.

industries.industry: Municipal utilities, electric co-ops, and local governments
industries.note: These entities would gain a clear federal right to offer broadband even in states that currently prohibit it. Any revenue they earn would come from providing service to residents, often where private providers will not build.
